utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can, even though I did not hear any translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if you couldn't hear any translation -- I am hearing the translation. Can you hear now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you receiving the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It's Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova, and Denise Gustin, case manager, as usual. Can I just briefly, before we deal with Mr. Ackerman's introductions, apologise for asking Your Honours for a decision we'd already got? We'd forgotten that you did an enormous decision which covered everything barring the Rule 92 witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was confused too when you mentioned it. Because I know I had discussed it but I had the legal officer over there and I wasn't quite sure whether it was him or someone else and he was looking at me, I was looking at him, and I couldn't remember. I mean, I got it actually confused at the time with the Rule 92, and I was -- I had some fixed ideas on what I had done and instructions I had given on the Rule 92 bis motion and I had forgotten about the other one completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've already apologised to the legal officer about it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, you don't need to apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. Appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin, I'm John Ackerman, along with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you too. Before we start, I have received a note this morning from the registry that the Eid Al Adha feast, holiday, which was indicated until this morning at least on my agenda to be -- to occur, to fall on Wednesday, the 12th February, is now on the 11th. That's Tuesday. So basically, we will be sitting on Wednesday but we will not be sitting on Monday -- on Tuesday. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have an action-packed week that week, I may say. Mr. Kirudja is going to be testifying. I've estimated he will take a whole day in chief and probably a day but -- so there will be that gap. And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But I just wanted to make sure you are aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I heard that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will not be sitting on Tuesday and we will be sitting instead on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm told it's a holiday that has something to do with the phases of the moon rather, like Easter. Presumably they didn't work out the moon phases properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Eid Al Adha. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a Muslim holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Eid Al Adha is an elaborate word meaning feast.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a Muslim holiday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Eid Al Adha is probably tomorrow. That's what it probably means. But I don't know any way. Eid Al Adha. So, good morning to you, sir. And welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We should conclude your cross-examination, I would say, very soon, but before we even start, please stand up. The usher will hand you again the text of the solemn declaration, repeat it and then Mr. Ackerman will be able to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You my sit down. Mr. Ackerman, open session or private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we start with open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, most of the questions that I have prepared to ask you, I think can be answered very simply. Many of them with just a simple yes or no. And if you can do that, then most assuredly we can finish rather soon so that you'll be free to depart. So let's see if we can accomplish that, shall we? Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday in your testimony about seeing helicopters and other aircraft flying around the Bosanski Novi area, and you guessed, I believe, that they might be supplying -- the helicopters at least might be supplying arms to the Serbian people. At that time, there was a war going on just across the border in Croatia, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And because of the fighting going on just across the border in Croatia, it was not unusual to see helicopters and aircraft involved in that fighting over there, flying in and around the border area at Bosanski Novi, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I would just like to clarify the situation at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The helicopters were coming from Prijedor area across the Kozara mountain and were skirting the city and would then fly across the Japra valley and an area called Krslje, Josava and other villages, where there was only Serb population. As to any other aircraft flying over the area coming from Croatia or any other battles going on, there was nothing of the sort at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you some questions about the statement that you gave to the Prosecutor on 5 May of the year 2000. I'd ask the Prosecutor to supply you a copy of it so you can follow along and be certain that I'm quoting it properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 5th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, 5 April, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During that interview, sir, with the OTP, you were asked about whether or not you were aware of any propaganda going on in the Bosanski Novi area. I'm referring to page 3 in the English version. It's a paragraph beginning with the language, "I don't know of any propaganda." And what the English indicates you said was this: "I don't know of any propaganda apart from Chetnik songs played on the radio. I do remember speeches made by various political figures such as Karadzic, Kupresanin, and Seselj." And it talks a little bit about, "The speeches were not much different than other Serb politicians'." That's what you said, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should find that passage quoting my declaration. I can't do it that fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to get you some help.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might even be missing from my papers -- no, no, no. I've just found it. On page 3, no propaganda except for the Chetnik songs being played on the radio. What I meant was the media propaganda which would not be accessible to the other side, because at that time, well, we knew in whose hands the radio station of Bosanski Novi was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday in your testimony, sir, you mentioned a group called dry ribs, Suha Rebra. You described them as --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- having been involved in torture slaughter, burning, forcing people to jump off buildings apparently and things of that nature. Do you know where this group was from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were they from the Bosanski Novi area or were they from across the river in the Dvor area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of Bosanski Novi, the outskirts of Bosanski Novi, an area called Tunjica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, during your testimony, page 80 of the LiveNote, you were asked the following question: "Q. Were you aware and can you just answer me this question, please, yes or no? Were you aware of a Regional Crisis Staff in Banja Luka?" The answer you gave was: "A. I had heard rumours but as to whether Pasic consulted with them, well, I don't know." Do you remember giving that testimony yesterday, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor back in April of the year 2000, you were asked, were you not, if you were aware of a Regional Crisis Staff and you answered, "I am not aware of a Regional Crisis Staff." That was your answer, sir, and you will find that I think on the same page 3, just one paragraph above the earlier paragraph about propaganda. It's the bottom of page 2, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bottom of page 2, sir. Bottom of page 2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, because it says Regional Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that's the truth, isn't it? You were never aware of a Regional Crisis Staff at the time, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, no. I knew that there was a Crisis Staff in Banja Luka, but as to whether it was called Regional Crisis Staff, I don't know, even though it would basically be logical that it would be called that way because of the administrative divisions and levels in this area, so it would have had to be a Regional Crisis Staff. I suppose it was called Crisis Staff for the area of Banja Luka, and the neighbouring areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I assume you're aware that there was a municipal Crisis Staff covering the municipality of Banja Luka, just like the municipal Crisis Staff of Bosanski Novi covered the area of Bosanski Novi. Weren't you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every municipality had a Crisis Staff. I suppose there were subregional levels as well, and probably Regional Crisis Staff for the entire area of Banja Luka, the Banja Luka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about listening to the radio or watching television and said you did that "when we had electricity or could find batteries." Can you tell us how much of the time during the year 1992 you did not have electricity and therefore could not watch television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite some time has elapsed since then. You should be aware, Your Honour, that all my notes, quotes and figures, all my papers have been taken away from my house. My house has been searched on a number of occasions, and I didn't actually keep records. I wasn't able to do so, so I can't tell you exactly how many times that we had power cuts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Or expecting you to be precise to the dot. I mean, it's just -- how frequently? Say once a week, twice a week, once a month, more than once a month? Once a year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly two to three times a week, we had some weeks when we did not have power cuts but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Does that satisfy you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know why there were power cuts? Do you know why there were these problems with electricity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is it the case that you had power sometimes gone two or three days a week and you never made inquiry as to why this was happening, what was it that was causing these power problems?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not obtain any information because the phones owned by Bosniaks had been disconnected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your answer is that you never asked anybody and never found out why these power problems occurred in Bosanski Novi in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in touch with quite a few Serbs, my neighbours for example, next door neighbours, and they didn't know either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Batteries apparently were also hard to find during this period of 1992. Is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. Some people found it easy to get batteries and others didn't. I wasn't one of the lucky ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you were able to get batteries, where did you -- where did you get? Where could find batteries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the news agents or in some shops or maybe through a shopkeeper whom we knew, who could sell us certain articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday about Mr. Brdjanin. On page 26 of the transcript at line 22, you had this to say: "I think that he had some leading positions but I don't know exactly what his job was." Now, sir, the fact is you have no idea what his position was, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he told us yesterday that -- I think he told us yesterday that he doesn't know for sure, hasn't got an idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I just quoted what he said, and I think it's a bit vague: "I don't know exactly what his job was."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what I want to ask is: You have no idea what his job was? It's not that you're confused, but you don't know what it is, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't like to be quoted as saying I have no idea about something. I think there is more appropriate language that could be used as well. I said I did not know exactly what the position of Mr. Brdjanin was but that it was a position pretty high up in the hierarchy within the SDS party, well, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how is it that you know that? What causes you to conclude that he had a position high in the hierarchy of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I had the honour and the possibility to watch television, well, for the most part of that period, it was out of order even when we did not have power cuts, and I was listening to the radio as well, so I found out a certain number of things in relation to Mr. Brdjanin as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We spoke a little bit earlier about your having -- whether or not you heard any propaganda, and that's on page 3 of your statement to the OTP, and I read this to you a few moments ago but I'll read it to you again, sir. What you said was: "I remember speeches made by various political figures such as Karadzic, Kupresanin, and Seselj." That's what you told the OTP in April of the year 2000, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was your sense of the position held by Mr. Kupresanin? Was that a high-level position, or if you know exactly what his position was, could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this much: He held one of the higher positions. I don't know which position exactly. But I do know that he was well respected and held in high esteem by certain people from the Crisis Staff, and certain citizens I know -- in fact, certain citizens I knew, and knew rather well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you talked there in your statement, when you spoke to the OTP about the various political figures whose speeches you had heard, you did not mention Mr. Brdjanin, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said earlier that I never contacted Mr. Brdjanin personally, never talked to him directly, never attended any meetings together with him, and all I know were the things I could learn at some point about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever talk with Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Kupresanin or Mr. Seselj personally or attend any meetings where they appeared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank heavens I didn't attend any meetings where they appeared, but I do know that both Karadzic and Kupresanin visited Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said in your testimony yesterday at page 27, beginning at line 3, referring to Mr. Brdjanin, "It was my judgement that after all, he was somebody who was consulted and was probably involved in the decision-making processes due to his position within the party." If you have a basis for making that kind of a judgement, could you please tell the Trial Chamber what it is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really have to make one thing clear: Before the war began, I was a deputy in the assembly of Yugoslavia. Before the war, I often visited Banja Luka. I knew many politicians and renowned people from all walks of life in Banja Luka. I was aware that Banja Luka was a regional administrative centre from which all initiatives and ideas issued, including instructions about what subordinate units, administrative units, should do. This is why I assumed, in view of the high position of Mr. Brdjanin, that he had a say in things and he must have been consulted about certain decisions that were made between Crisis Staffs of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, you indicated, although he was not one of the persons named in your statement to the OTP, that you'd heard making speeches, that you heard that -- you had heard Mr. Brdjanin speaking on television and you said, "I believe in one of the speeches there was a reference to moving the Muslims out of the area. Something like that." It's the case, isn't it, that you have very little memory of this programme that you claim to have seen Mr. Brdjanin on, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said, if I remember well, was the following: I came back home, I don't know exactly at what time, but in time for -- to see the end of the television programme where one could hear Mr. Brdjanin's speech but I asked one neighbour to tell me about it, and explain it to me, and as far as I understood the explanation, it was about how relationships would shift and what should be done with the Banja Luka Corps. I did not hear or read Mr. Brdjanin's speech in its entirety, nor did I have the opportunity to watch a retransmission of the speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So having not seen it, you first of all don't know specifically what the person said, and you can't even say with certainty that it was Mr. Brdjanin and not some other politician, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that this speech was broadcast, because I saw Mr. Brdjanin on television, but that time I came back from work late, [redacted], and I came back home in time to hear the end of the speech. I don't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. It's good that the microphone wasn't on. Madam Registrar, make a printout of this page, please, and I will tell you what to redact. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You want to turn your mic off again now, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that the Bosanski Novi municipality, you agreed with some figures read to you by Ms. Korner, in the 1991 census was about 60 per cent Serb. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the multi-party elections, it's the case, isn't it, that the SDS won the majority of the seats in the Bosanski Novi municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's how it was, too, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the proportional representation was observed in terms of percentages. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you do know that the SDS won the majority of seats in the municipal assembly, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It held the key positions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The President of the municipality was a Serb and a member of the SDS, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, Ms. Korner kept asking you about the takeover of Bosanski Novi. Who was it that took over what from whom? The Serbs were already holding the key positions and were the majority government because of the elections. So what kind of a takeover was there, if any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an absolute coup, removing Bosniaks from all public positions and making it impossible to continue with normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But this -- this business of removing Bosniaks from public positions, that resulted, did it not, from an election that was held where the SDS won the majority and therefore were in control of the government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS controlled all key positions, but you were asking me about the coup. It was effected by the SDS and its part pardon sans.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we have exhausted that. We need to go to private session now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement to the Prosecutor, if you'll move down from that part that talks about medical supplies coming from Banja Luka about two paragraphs, it's indicated that you told the Prosecutor the following: "There was a group of Bosnian intellectuals that went to meet local authorities. They suggested that the majority of Bosniaks should move because of incidents and -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to be able to find the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Next page, second paragraph -- no, not two pages over, just one. "There was a group of Bosnian intellectuals."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "There was a group of Bosnian intellectuals that went to meet local authorities. They suggested that the majority of Bosniaks should move because of incidents and that it was not good for them to stay in Bosanski Novi. As far as probably I know, this was the initiative of the Bosniaks. They asked for the presence of international agencies to be present. I don't think that either the Serbs or the Bosnians expected so many people to move out that same day." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, and the group of Muslim intellectuals went to negotiate with the municipal authorities in relation to the possibility of their moving out of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But, sir, my question is: What you told the Office of the Prosecutor that day, you continue to stand by, do you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I maintain that there was a group of Muslims, Bosniaks, asking for some of the Muslims to be moved out of Bosanski Novi for security reasons, safety reasons. I am still sticking to that original statement. That was the gist of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Just -- I just want to have this made very clear, sir, so let me ask it this way. You see the paragraph that begins with, "There was a group," and ends with, "Bosnians expected so many people to move out that same day." You have found that paragraph. Read that paragraph and tell me if you stand by what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And "stand by" means for every part of that paragraph. Because although the whole -- the entire paragraph was read out to you by Mr. Ackerman, the subsequent -- your subsequent answer did not cover the entirety of it but only part of it. So go through the paragraph, let's go through it sentence by sentence if necessary, and just confirm whether you stand by it or not. I'll do that myself, Mr. Ackerman. First, "There was a group of Bosnian intellectuals that went to meet local authorities. They suggested that the majority of Bosniaks should move because of incidents and that" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was not good for them to stay in Bosanski Novi. Do you stand by this? Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And then you also say, "As far as I know, this was the initiative of the Bosniaks." Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you add, "They asked for the presence of international agencies to be present." Do you stand by there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to provide guarantees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And then finally, you conclude by saying, "I don't think that either the Serbs or Bosnians expected so many people to move out that same day." Do you agree, do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We need to go back to private session again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Ms. Korner, is there re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, in fact in relation to that last answer, but I think I can deal with that without having to go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, from what you've just said, you do not know whom Mr. Pasic went to consult? You just know that he went to consult someone or some body, some body of people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose he must have consulted someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's all I ask in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Sir, we have some questions from the bench, after which you would have earned your rest for the rest of the week at least. Judge Taya?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: On page 3, in paragraph 2 of your statement, 5 April, 2000, you stated that, "I heard that Mr. Brdjanin came to the municipality -- municipal building several times." My question is as follows: First one, you mean the municipality building of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: From whom you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my neighbours, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Approximately when you heard about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT81 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't state it categorically as having been in 1992, but I did hear that he came in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So, sir, that brings us to the end of your testimony in this trial, for which I thank you. I also thank you for having accepted to come over. I know this wasn't easy for you. I can put your mind at rest that you will be attended to by the officials of this Tribunal to assist you for -- on your return to your country of residence. I thank you once more and you will now be escorted by the usher. Ms. Korner, we have a quarter of an hour. Shall we start straight away with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Richterova is calling the next witness. I can't recall if there are any protective measures, there are not so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no protective measures so members of the gallery, we will soon be starting with another witness so the curtains being drawn shouldn't deter you from -- they came to follow the proceedings, most of which were in private session, and they were trying to get a glimpse of who was getting -- giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. Your Honour, I find this slightly unnerving because I notice some gentleman wandering around yesterday who was trying to look around. I think they ought to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, Madam Registrar, please, make sure that when we are in private or -- private session, that the monitors at the back -- I know that you did take precautions yesterday, but some of them were trying to find out exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Richterova points out that in fact although it's slightly early it makes sense to take the break now and start the new witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have -- yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might ask Your Honours if I could be excused for the balance of this session so I could do some other tasks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are excused Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is taking over?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Me too, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You too? So it's Madam Richterova will be conducting the chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: She will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher, please could you bring the witness in, the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to disturb but I can hear you. This document is only in B/C/S. It's an exhumation report, and I will use it at the end only for confirmation of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I received this document this morning, so I hope that there won't be any objection that this document is only in its original language. I already asked the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Trbojevic, I understand that there wouldn't be any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The gentleman who is standing next to you will be handing to you the text of a solemn declaration. This is the equivalent of an oath. That means a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. So now I invite to you read that solemn declaration aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Trial Chamber as explained to you by me already. So please proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. You may sit down. Please be seated. Usher, please arrange the microphones. Thank you. Mr. Alic, I will explain to you very briefly what's going to happen here. We will start with a series of questions that will be put to you by Madam Richterova, who is in charge of the Prosecution today. And when she is finished with her questions, you will then be cross-examined, in other words asked a few questions, by Mr. Trbojevic, who is co-counsel defending Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, who is the accused in this case. Then we'll see whether it's the case of a re-examination, some further questions, either from the Prosecution or from the bench. I am the Presiding Judge, my name is Agius and I come from Malta, and on my right you can see Judge Janu from the Czech Republic, and on my left, Judge Taya from Japan. I thank you, Madam Richterova you can start with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, would you be so kind and state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I'm Alic, Midho.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were born on 7 February, 1955 in Blagaj, Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: In 1955 in Blagaj Japra, which is in the municipality of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you are a Bosniak; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, I would like to start by showing you a map of Bosanski Novi municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to show the witness P1624.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you show us at this map where Blagaj Japra is?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Opposite of Blagaj Japra is Blagaj Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, across the river Sana.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it correct to state that these two villages have one name, Blagaj or they are known as Blagaj, and the village Blagaj is --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: -- divided by the river Sana into Blagaj Rijeka and Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who lived in these two villages? What was the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: In Blagaj Japra, there lived only Muslims. In Blagaj Rijeka there were both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many people lived in these -- how many Muslims lived in these two villages?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: In Blagaj Japra, there were approximately 500 households, maybe 2.000 people in all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you look at the map, you can see other villages, and can you tell us which of these villages were occupied by Bosniaks, by Muslims? And if you can point --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you that there were Muslims here in Hozici as well and in Donji Agici [Realtime transcript read in error "Maglici"], and there were Serbs. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the speaker should speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: And in Gornji Agici, there were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just for the record, it's not "Maglici" but Agici?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Agici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What other areas were occupied by primarily by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand, whether within the municipality of Bosanski Novi or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, no. We will talk only about the municipality of Bosanski Novi. So I will ask you, was Ekici and Alici Muslim village or Serb?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: It was a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Crna Rijeka and Hodzici?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Crna Rijeka, there were both Serbs and Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you tell us the closest Serbian village which was to Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Petkovac which is not indicated here, and then Svodna. It was a Serb village as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what about Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Maslovare had a mixed population, both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I am done with the map for the time. I want to ask you about the life in Blagaj Japra. You said that it was primarily a Muslim village, but did you have contact with villages -- with Serb villages? And now I'm talking before 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How would you briefly describe the relationship between Serb and non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Before the war, the relations were quite good. We went to school together. We sat in the classroom together. There were no problems at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you socialise?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said before the war. Do you -- and you mean the war in Croatia which started in --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In 1991. Now, I want to ask you in which way the life change after the war started?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. First Muslims who had jobs in companies were being dismissed, and then slogans started appearing, Serbia and all that, and posters of Slobodan Milosevic, and all the insignia. And if you went to see a doctor, you could get a prescription for the necessary medicines but if you were a Muslim, you couldn't get the medicines and if you were a Serb, you could. So we didn't enjoy the same rights as they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will stop you here for a moment, and we will go step by step. You mentioned that if -- that people lost their jobs, first Muslims who had jobs in companies were being dismissed. Let's start with dismissal. What can you tell us, to your knowledge, what do you know about these dismissals?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I had a friend, Mesinovic, Mustafa, who was told one day, when he appeared for work, to go home. There was no work for him to do any more. And then other people in my village found themselves in the same situation. I did not have a job myself so I was not dismissed, but for the most part it was the Muslims who were losing their jobs, both from the businesses or other official positions as civil servants.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned civil servants. Do you have some example of a civil servant who would be Muslim and dismissed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I don't know personally, but I did hear that they were losing their jobs. I can't think of any names in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I will move to -- to your knowledge, was there any restriction of movement in Bosanski Novi municipality? And now I'm talking about -- let's start -- the beginning of 1992, spring 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a curfew.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How did you learn about this curfew?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, on the radio, and we were told that between 8.00 and 12.00, you were not allowed to be out or 2.00 to 4.00 or 5.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Are you saying that you were not allowed to be on the street between 8.00 in the morning and 12.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then in the afternoon, after 12.00 or rather 2.00, and then afterwards. So basically, you were simply allowed out to buy groceries or whatever, or feed the animals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there any difficulty to go from your village, Blagaj Japra, to the town of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs were free to move about. The Muslims were not. Yes, certainly, there must have been cases but I don't know. I mean some people risked it and sometimes they were either not recognised or not seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If I understand you said yes, but tell me, do you know whether there were any checkpoints which would check movement of people out of Blagaj Japra or whether there were some checkpoints in the vicinity of the town of Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of Bosanski Novi, sometimes there were moved to Blagaj Rijeka because that's on the road to Prijedor and Banja Luka. They would be moved there temporarily and then somewhere else as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you personally go through these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I myself didn't, because I was self-employed. I had my own business, and I could not get more fuel to go and get the commodities. So I sold everything out and then I couldn't get any fuel, I couldn't work any more, I couldn't move anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will elaborate on one thing. At the beginning you mentioned that Muslims cannot get medicine, but Serbs were able to get it.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was there any -- was there ever a refusal by shops in town to serve or supply foodstuffs to the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not in my case but some of my neighbours, yes. I mean, they didn't have groceries and then they went to look for them and then, yes, they got them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But do you know what kind of food or what kind of stuff they were refused to be sold?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: For the most part, it was foodstuffs, flour, salt, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, was there barracks in Bosanski Novi town?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know what type of unit was there stationed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. For the most part, I observed reservists, not really young people, who went in and out of the barracks, armed, mostly of Serbian ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now what year are you talking about, when you mention these reservists?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, even before the war, while the war was going on in Croatia, there were reservists and they stayed on when the war began in Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after the war started, and during the first half of the year 1992, was the situation the same? Was there reservists or were there regular soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: There were mostly reservists at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: These reservists, did they come to your village? I know I'm now -- I'm sorry, I'm again talking about the first half of the year 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they come officially or did they just went through?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I don't believe they came officially because I had both a small shop and a restaurant. They would come in to my catering establishment to drink and eat. I don't know on what basis they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the war in Croatia, were there occasions that soldiers with equipments would pass through your village?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How often did it happen?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Sometimes it was every day. Sometimes in other periods it was every other day. Depends.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what can you tell me about the soldiers who passed through your village? Who were they and how did they behave?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: For the most part, they were all the soldiers, reservists, they were rowdy, they shot in the air, they shot at the mosque, they saw a mosque and immediately knew it was a Muslim village. She showed the three-finger sign, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In -- at the end of 1991, first half of 1992, are you aware of the fact that Serbs would be receiving weapons, or that they would be arming themselves?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, we did know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you personally see anything?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Through Blagaj Japra and the valley of the Japra, every other day trucks would be passing loaded, and you could feel when the truck was full, loaded, the engine would work in a certain way, and you knew when it came back empty, the engine would work differently, the sound was different, and these trucks carried weapons and ammunition that belonged previously to the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did these trucks, were they military trucks?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively military trucks. There were also civilian trucks passing but for the most part, there were military trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But you didn't see, personally, what was in these trucks?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it with my own eyes but I suppose it was military equipment. Why would they be carrying something else on army trucks? Army helicopters landed in Serbian villages, such as Vladimirovic, Svodna, Maslovare, exclusively areas populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see these helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It would land, remain on the ground for half an hour, an hour, and then take off again. I didn't see what they carried or what they unloaded, but I could see they landed only in Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to deal with a document which was premarked as Exhibit P1656. And I know that the witness -- if I'm not wrong -- has slight difficulty to read because of his injury in his eye. I would read passages from this document, and ask him to make comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, it would be better if he is still given the text, and if it could be of any help to him, we could put it on the ELMO, the Serbo-Croat version of the text, and have it zoomed so that it will more visible to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: For the interpreters, now I'm referring to the page 2, second page, the last paragraph, starting in Serbian language [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the English version if I read you well, it's the bottom of page 3, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's bottom of page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, you may even look on the screen, if it is easier for you to read it, and this is a wrong page. It should be page 2. Yeah, yeah, exactly. And I will read you one paragraph, and then I will ask you to make a comment. It says, "SDA activists, planned and prepared groups to destroy the bridge over the Sana River in Blagaj and the Japra river in Petkovac in case the organs of the military police intervene and carried out repressive measures." SDA activists commented on this in public in Blagaj. And now I'm interested in fact in this part, "Through operational work, information was obtained that the people listed below possessed automatic weapons and hand grenades, the distribution of which was organised by the SDA in the course of January 1992." And then we have a list of 20 names, and I -- you saw this list yesterday, and I asked you whether you knew these people. My first question is: What do you know about arming Muslims in the village of Blagaj Japra or Blagaj Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about it. And I suppose that it is not true, that it is propaganda and sheer lies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you want to -- do you want to say that there were no weapons at all in Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. Apart from the weapons we had licences for, meaning hunting rifles, carbines, and pistols.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So there were weapons but they were legal -- legally-obtained weapons, like pistols or hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, only that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Under number 4, his name Ismet Selimovic. Did you know this person?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: He was the secretary of the local commune of Blagaj Japra and Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document says that he was in possession of automatic weapon, among others. Do you know whether -- to your knowledge, was he in possession of automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't. I know he had a pistol, a Bereta, just as I did, because I know I borrowed bullets from him but we only had licensed weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Richterova, could you ask him whether he was related to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just intended to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was Ismet Selimagic related to you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. He was my brother-in-law or son-in-law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note. It is not quite clear in our language which it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you describe what was the relationship because the interpreter cannot get the right words. Was he a husband of your daughter or a daughter of your brother?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes it even more confusing, Madam Richterova, daughter of your brother? How was he related to you? By blood or by marriage?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our language, that means that he was married to the daughter of my step-brother, not my own daughter but the daughter of my step-brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay that's clear enough. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or half-brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I want to move to the page in B/C/S, it is page 3, and it is third paragraph starting. [B/C/S spoken] this on the top. And in English language, it is page 5, in the middle of the page. And I will read again. "Towards the end of March, in the area of Blagaj Rijeka, a military equipment was distributed to members of the SDA armed forces, uniforms and berets, with two emblems, one of which was a yellow star with a crescent and the other the old Bosnian coat of arms, which is worn by members of the League of Patriots." Are you aware of the fact that the members of SDA were distributing such uniforms, either in Blagaj Rijeka or Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody got that. Nobody received that. And that too is an untruth. In other words a lie.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any Muslim armed forces in Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. There was nothing. Nobody wore a uniform in Blagaj Japra or in Blagaj Rijeka, and in the entire valley of the Japra river, nobody was wearing even a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now I will read the final part. It is again on this page 3, and it is in the middle, the paragraph starts, [B/C/S spoken] and I will read it from the third line, and in English, it is page 6, and it starts, third line from the top. And it says, "SDA activists in Blagaj step up the subversive propaganda activity by reinforcing the opinion among the Muslim public that it was essential to fight until the final liberation from the Serbs. They thus spread a negative attitude amongst its people towards the army and the Serbs and prepared psychologically for the beginning of the conflict. This culminated in an attack on a military police patrol from the Banja Luka Corps which was passing through Blagaj on 10 or 11 May of this year." And the last sentence: "Since the SDA did not respect the agreement reached by the municipal assembly on disarming paramilitary formations, and an attack on a military police patrol in Blagaj followed, disarmament was also carried out by partially searching the field." I want to ask you a few questions about what I just read. Are you aware of any type of Muslim propaganda within Blagaj which would be raised by any leading members of SDA in this area?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. There was none.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us who -- who were the leading members of SDA in your village?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I know about Izet Mehmedagic, only about him, but no one else in my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you heard anything which would promote hatred towards Serbs in your village?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: You mean on the part of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there anyone who would ask, request, people to arm themselves and fight against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there anyone who would ask Muslims to be tolerant, not to -- not to provokate anyone?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: You mean somebody who asked Muslims to refrain from provoking Serbs or the other way around?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. Was there anyone among Muslims who would ask, who would request, other Muslims not to provokate the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, we were all in favour of not provoking anyone. All to the last man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there you are not answering the question. You're telling us that you were all more or less in agreement amongst yourselves that you shouldn't provoke the Serbs, in other words that you should or that you would rather keep sleeping dogs lying. The question is: Amongst the Muslim leadership, was there any initiative to encourage the Muslims in Blagaj to be passivists, to be tolerant and not to provoke the Serbs? Was there an initiative coming from the top or was it just something that you felt naturally amongst you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was no initiative from outside. It came from within. All we asked for was to be left alone and we were happy to leave everyone else alone. There was no one who came from outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I will not ask about the person who would come from the outside. And I will be more specific. We already mentioned Ismet Selimagic. Do you remember that Ismet Selimagic would talk about the life between Muslims and Serbs, how it should be arranged?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: He didn't say anything about that. He, too, was in favour of everybody leaving everyone else alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will move with this document. We mentioned or I mentioned or this document mentioned that there was an attack on a military police patrol on 10 or 11 May. Do you know whether something like that really happened?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. An incident happened but it was not created by Muslims. Serbs themselves orchestrated this incident. And in Zurim, between Bosanski Novi and Blagaj, they threw a hand grenade on a military jeep, fired a couple of bursts of gunfire, turned on all the lights on the vehicle, and headed forward, and they were saying that it was the Muslims who did it, whereas that wasn't true. They themselves orchestrated this incident to make it look otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the date, the date, is it correct that it happened on 10 or 11 May this year, which means 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: It was the 11th. The 11th of May at 10.00 p.m., around 10.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document further states that the SDA did not respect the agreement on disarming. I will deal with this in a moment. For the moment, I'm done with the document. Thank you. Mr. Alic, in spring, do you remember any announcement with respect to handing over, surrender of weapons in Blagaj?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And do you recall when was it?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I remember. It was on the -- give me just a second to remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it before --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: It was sometime around the 6th of May, when the Radio Bosanski Novi broadcast an ultimatum to the Muslims to hand over any weapons they had, not later than the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you just said that you heard it over the Radio Bosanski Novi. Do you still recall this announcement, who did this announcement? Was it some -- was it the police or municipal assembly or SDS or SDA, whoever, that he -- that this organisation would ask people to surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Serbian -- Serb Crisis Staff in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after the announcement that you have to surrender weapons, what was your reaction, people in your village? Did you surrender the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We were happy to turn our weapons over, but we could only turn over the weapons we possessed with the licence. And they wanted us to hand over something that we didn't have at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you said you decided to hand over the weapons. Where were you supposed to take these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: They required us to bring our weapons in front of the assembly of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You are talking about assembly in the town of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you go separately or did you -- did you choose one person from your village who would take these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We gathered in front of the school building in Blagaj Japra, the last day before the end of the ultimatum. It was the 11th, a Sunday, and we agreed to turn over all we had to Izet Mehmedagic because he was president of the SDA or a member of the SDA, I'm not sure. Izet had a small truck and he loaded all the weapons we had into his truck and drove it to the building of the assembly in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And do you know -- you didn't obviously -- you didn't go with him but did you later learn what happened when he -- Izet Mehmedagic brought these weapons in front of the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: After Izet loaded the weapons on his truck and drove off, we remained standing in front of the school building to hear how it would all proceed and how it would end.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah. And you again didn't answer my question. What did you learn, if anything, from Izet Mehmedagic, after he returned to the village? Did he hand over the weapons or what happened with these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, he took the weapons there. We waited for him to come back. And when he did, he came back with the same weapons and he told us to collect our weapons because they simply laughed at him and they said, "Take it back. That's not what we want. You didn't deliver what we asked you to deliver."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And as you already said a couple of seconds ago, it is at the same night this military police car was attacked?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell us, after the military car was attacked, what happened? What happened that night in your village?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: After the attack, I was sitting in front of my house and I was smoking. The first shells were fired on to Blagaj Japra, 13 shells, and we heard other firearms but basically there were 13 shells landing in Blagaj Japra.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did the shelling last?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Approximately half an hour, maybe one hour. They didn't follow closely one another. They would fire two or three shells and then wait a bit and a couple of shells again and wait again. Perhaps between 30 minutes and a hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you able to see whether -- what -- whether there was something specific targeted?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We couldn't see. We could simply hear the shells landing. We could approximately tell where it had landed. One landed not too far from my house, maybe 50 or 100 metres away but we didn't know what the targets were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said the shelling lasted approximately one hour, which would mean that the shelling would stop shortly after midnight. Did anything else happen between midnight and the following morning?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Nothing happened during the night. I with my wife and children and my neighbours, about ten families altogether, we were hiding in a cellar and waited for the morning to find out what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in the morning, did you find out what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. We just heard it on the radio that there was a -- yet another call for the arms to be surrendered, a repeat of that original call that we had a couple of days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And this morning, after you heard that there was another call to surrender the arms, did you discuss the situation among themselves and maybe with your Serb neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, not with the Serbs. We had planned a convoy to go to the town hall with our tractors, our vehicles, to take those weapons back to them but they rejected it. First of all, they told us to do so, and then they let us know that the road between Blagaj and Bosanski Novi was closed and so not to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This following day, was there another shelling of your town, of your village?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as they made that announcement, about an hour earlier, another round of shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long this particular shelling lasted?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: That lasted a bit longer, let's say between 10.00 in the morning until early afternoon, 1.00 or 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And because it was daylight, were you able to see whether they targeted any specific buildings?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. We couldn't because as soon as the shelling started, we left Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for the shelters, I mean the same cellar that we spent the night in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after the shelling stopped or maybe during, did you receive any information that you should move to another village?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, not yet, but my father and my uncles and Alic, Amil, and a couple of other people agreed amongst themselves to go to the neighbouring village called Vitezovac to talk to the Serbs and ask what it was all about, since the road to Bosanski Novi was closed, to find out what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what did they find?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: They went to Drago Ninic. Since he had a coffee shop, he opened the doors for them. So they went in and he -- no. They went to negotiate things, and he -- no, my father said to him to serve them a drink. He said, "Drago bring us a drink." And he answered my father, "No, no, no, Jasim, I can't give you a drink any more. That was in 9 old days but we can't drink together any longer".

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And this is what you later learned from your father?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: When he came back home, that's what he told us. But they had barely reached the house and the shelling started again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And during this shelling, did you decide to move to another village?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. My neighbour, Selmic, Hamdija, came on his tractor, and he came to my part of the village. He more or less knew which houses had cellars and so on, and even with the shelling and all, he came along and he told us all to come out of the shelters and to tell the others that we should form a convoy and go to Rajko Hodzic in Maslovare.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you go to Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We all went, all of us. I mean some people stayed in the woods, and some people stayed back in the cellars. We didn't know about them. We thought they had left as well so we went to Maslovare. And as we were approaching Maslovare, near Mica Karlica's house there were about a dozen Serbs. There was a ramp barring our way and that's where they were waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will stop you here for a second. You mentioned Mica Karlica and some other Serbs. What did they -- what did they wear? Were they in uniforms or in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: They wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what kind of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Army fatigue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: All of them. They all had automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Apart from Mica Karlica, did you know any -- anybody else from this group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Whom did you know?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I knew Ranko Gvozden, Milan Gvozden, Djuro Miljatovic, Mico Baltic, and some others. There were more of them. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: From Maslovare.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And before I stopped you, you said that they were waiting for you. So tell us what happened after they stopped you.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: When we got to the checkpoint, I was in the first tractor with Hamdija Selmic. I got off and Mico Karlica -- well, the convoy stopped and Mico Karlica asked me whether we had any weapons and we said yes, and he says, "Well, inform everybody and surrender your arms and leave everything to us."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I myself went along the convoy and asked the people bearing arms to take them to the checkpoint and surrender their weapons, and that's what they did. For the most part, those were handguns and guns -- and carbines.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did -- after this, did you reach Maslovare, the village of Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: They directed us in the direction of Rajko Hodzica's holding. He was a rich man and had a large holding and big stables, and so we could go to his stables and his garage and his outhouses and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We spent a night there, and we stayed until approximately 10.00 in the morning. Then the Serb soldiers bearing arms came along, five or six of them, and they inquired about Mehinovic, Huso, in particular and some other people as well. I can't remember the names exactly. And Camil Azic answered and then they said that Huso had a grenade launcher or rather a mortar and apparently he had not surrendered it. And the other guy said well, I can tell you he does not have it. I could swear that he does not have the mortar, I can swear on my head. And they said, "Well, you think your life is very cheap."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you -- you said you stayed there over night and the following day were you able to return to Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. When they collected some of our people, some Bosniaks, and they left in the direction of Blagaj to search everything, and to see whether everything was empty and safe, but they put our people in front of them, the Muslims, and they said, "If anybody decides to shoot us, you will all get killed."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So at the end, did you return to Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't at that stage. They first went to Blagaj and checked the area and they put their flag on a big house - I can't remember what house exactly, what was the name of it - and on the stables belonging to Refik Uzeirovic and they placed the Serb flags there and they said whoever interferes with these flags is going to be killed, just to make sure that nobody would interfere, and then they came back and they said you're free to go back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So eventually, you came home?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I had not relinquished my gun, and then Mico Karlica stopped me on the road as I was going back home. And he said to me -- because they had a list from the interior ministry and the police, about who had guns, and he reprimanded me because of that. And I said well, I will let you have the gun by nightfall. So I went back home, I looked for my gun, I found it, and I went back to Maslovare. I gave him the gun and I turned it in my direction so that he would not get the suspicion that I was going to shoot him or anything, and I got the cartridges out and -- well, he got the cartridges out, and he gave them back to me and I said "well, I don't need them." And he said, "I don't need them either." And then he put them in his pocket and then I went back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, now I want you to tell me briefly, when you returned back to Blagaj Japra, what did you see in the village? Was there anything -- everything in order or was anything destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. And I've forgotten to mention this. When I took the gun back, he offered me a beer, and I said, "Don't offer me drinks." I mean, we had been friends earlier on, so I said, "I don't feel like anything much." I had not had anything to eat or drink and I couldn't sleep the night. And then he made me have this beer and they were celebrating, they are were singing songs. I didn't mind, and then they made me have another beer so I had another beer. And then I asked Mico, "Could I go back -- could I go to the shop, could I go to the loo because I had two beers?" And then he said, no, go behind there. And then, as I was standing behind an outhouse, I happened to look inside, because there was a crack in the planks and so there was this crack, so one could see through about a centimetre or two, I could see inside. And I could see that this was full of army supplies, ammunitions, boxes, weapons, I can't remember exactly but it was full to the bursting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you for this information, but I will return back to my previous question. In which condition was Blagaj Japra and Blagaj Rijeka when you returned that day from Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, when I left Maslovare I could see that there were houses on fire from Vuco Mehanovica [phoen] then the mosque in Blagaj Japra, in Blagaj Rijeka, rather, and there was another house on fire there, and some other houses.
