I can't remember which ones exactly. According to my knowledge, this mosque in Blagaj Rijeka was set on fire by a Serb, Jovo - just a moment - Paukovic from the neighbouring village called Petkovac. After setting it on fire, he jumped into the water and he drowned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, just make it clear, there was a mosque in Blagaj Rijeka and there was a mosque in Blagaj Japra. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you just said that the mosque in Blagaj Rijeka was burning, that this --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was already burning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what about the minaret of that mosque?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: It was an old, wooden mosque, and it was on fire, so everything was on fire. There was no concrete or cement there, so everything was burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the mosque in Blagaj Japra, in which condition was this one?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: The minaret was still standing but it had been hit by several shells maybe, I don't know. I suppose it must have been a recoilless gun or something, because the shell went straight through the minaret and then out on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I will ask you about events which occurred between this day and 9 of June. In this short period of time, this month, were there shellings either of your village or other villages in Japra valley?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: In the subsequent fortnight, my village was fairly calm, perhaps even 20 days, but since we had phones, I heard that some other villages had been shelled, in much the same way as Blagaj and Rijeka Japra, villages such as Suhaca and Hodzici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you said that you learned over telephones that these villages were shelled. What happened to the population from these villages?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I suppose they must have fled somewhere during the shelling, or maybe had gone to shelters or cellars.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: My question was more about whether they stayed in these villages or whether they left these villages.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: They stayed for a while, and then it started in Gornji Agici and then Donji Agici, Suhaca, et cetera. They gradually started shelling all of those villages and chasing people away from their houses and chasing them in the direction of Blagaj so that the entire Japra valley was basically emptied and people were chased in the direction of Blagaj Japra and a part of Blagaj Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly how many people moved to Blagaj Japra and Blagaj Rijeka from these villages in Japra valley?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I suppose about 80.000 [as interpreted] people, including women and children. I can't tell you exactly how many inhabitants there were in each individual village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I just -- I'm not quite sure about the translation. Did you say 80, 80.000 or 18.000?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say 80. I said 8. 8.000. I said 8.000 to 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. So these people came to your village and they stayed for some period of time. During --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Now I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the time when these people from the Japra valley stayed in your village, were there any negotiations between Muslims or between SDA and Serb part, about the fate of these people?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sifet, who was the President of the SDA from Suhaca -- well, once every two or three days he travelled to Bosanski Novi to negotiate with the Serbs for people to return, et cetera, but it always seemed to fail. We still stayed where we were. There was a lot of uncertainty because we didn't know what would happen next. However, on the 8th of June, at around 4.00 in the afternoon, there was Mico Dolic and Ranko Gvozden who came along and they asked us to form a convoy at around 8.00, 9.00 in the morning and for us to go in the direction of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will again stop you here for a moment. You mentioned this person Sifet. Do you know his whole name?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I think it's Sifet Barjaktarevic. Barjaktarevic I think was his family name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you said he was president of the SDA from Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I stopped you when you mentioned that these three, two or three people came to your village, that you were -- that were you to form a convoy the following day. Who were these people? Were they soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Mico Dolic wore a uniform. Ranko Gvozden had the civilian top but he was wearing army camouflage pants, and both of them were of course armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when you said that this Mico Dolic wore a uniform, was it a military or police uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: A military, a soldier's uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So what happened on 9th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Since we could not believe it, nobody organised any convoys, we got up in the morning. In my house I had about 30 refugees from Suhaca, Hodzici, and some of the villages, and I myself with my family were staying at my parents' house. And we simply did not believe it, so we continued to sit at home and we were simply waiting. We didn't know what was going on. But then I went out into the street and there was Samid Imsirevic who had some knives and about a kilo or two kilos of meat from his butcher shop and he said there was a tank in the direction of Maslovare and there was a bus full of soldiers. And that made me a bit suspicious. I didn't say anything to anyone but it was suspicious.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At any point, did any soldiers come to your house?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. We could hear firearms. We were in the house. We didn't know what was going on, because that hamlet was a bit further away from the main road, and we were in the house when the shooting started and that they were shooting at our house, my father's house, and my mother went out and she could hear burning, and there was smoke. So as I was saying my mother went out of the house and she saw the army moving on to my parents' house, maybe five, six, ten soldiers, marching in the direction of the house, and they approached the house. And they said, Is there anything inside? And my mother gathered her courage and she went out and she said yes the house is full of people and then we were told to get out, and they swore at us and they told us to get out of the house, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you went out, there were these soldiers. Did you recognise any of --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the soldiers who approached your house?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Not at that point. I didn't recognise anyone. Some of them were wearing masks on their faces. Some of them didn't but I couldn't recognise anyone. As we came out, there was my brother, Kemal Alic and Ismet Selimagic. My brother, my mother, my wife, my four children. There were about 20 of us all in all. Maybe 25. I can't be precise now. They lined us all up against the barn, some of us, and against the hedge, some others. They cursed our mothers and told to us turn over our weapons. We said, We can't turn over any weapons because we had already turned them over in Maslovare. Since I had a disabled aunt, the wife of my uncle, they told us to go in the direction of the school building. Since we had this disabled woman with us, we had to carry her in our arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you enter the school building?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We arrived in front of the school building. There was a group of soldiers there. One soldier motioned us into the school building, and stayed with us all the time. The rest of the soldiers went behind the building, talking between themselves. We didn't know what they were talking about. Then they came back and told us to get out of the school building and go to the main road. We came out in a file and went. As soon as we came on to the main road from the yard, I saw a dead man lying on the road. He was lying face down. I couldn't see who it was. They told to us walk faster and not to look. Some 50 or 100 metres later, we saw a tank on the road and about 10 to 15 Serb soldiers around the tank.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw a dead body on the ground. What about houses? Were you able to observe what went on in the village?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We saw houses burning, hay stacks, stables, barns, smoke rising, although it was raining, but there was shooting from all sides, and everything was burning. You couldn't see where the shooting came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you saw a tank and soldiers. Did you -- did you go toward these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We did. And we passed by them and by the tank. Nobody told us a word. 50 metres on, we were going towards a hamlet, my hamlet, Sikare. A group of soldiers was waiting for us there. They were all armed. Some had masks on their faces, some didn't. I could recognise those who didn't have masks. They were waiting for us there, and they separated women and children on one side, and us men on the other side. My brother, Kemal Alic carried his 2-year-old son in his arms. And one of the soldiers took the child away from him and put the child into the other group giving it to the child's mother. Again, they demanded weapons. We said we don't have any. We had already turned it over. They said, "Throw on the ground everything you have in your pockets." We complied. We emptied our pockets. They asked Ismet Selimagic: "Where is your brother?" At first they asked who is the secretary in the local commune, and Ismet said, "I am." They asked, "Where is your brother?" He answered, "He is working in Zagreb." They said, "It's not true. He is in the Croat National Guard." And Ismet said, "It's not true. I can show you a paper." He motioned to get a paper from his jacket but he was not allowed to. The soldier hit him and he fell to the ground. Then another soldier came out, stepped out, and talked to my brother. I couldn't hear what they were saying. I was looking at my wife and children, who were crying out to me. I motioned to my wife to take the children further behind so that they should not look. So this other soldier came up to my brother and hit him three times in the head with a rifle butt. Nobody asked me anything. When we were throwing our documents on the ground, I asked one of Serbs, a big man who was wearing a hat with a Kokarda on his head, I asked him, "Can I keep my ID because it's an important document?" And the soldier answered, "No. You won't be needing it." At that point, I already knew that we wouldn't -- that we would come to a bad end, that something was in the offing. They released everyone else, my father, my uncle, every other man, except for me and my brother. Us, they lined up against the wall. I motioned to my wife to take the children away so that they wouldn't see what was going to happen, because I thought we were going to be executed. A soldier appeared who had a ski hat on his head so I could only see his face. He said, "Let these two men go because they didn't do anything." This man with the Kokarda looked at me, sized me up from head to toe, and told him to -- told me to go. This man was Milos Popovic. So I went off. One man was guarding my family under an awning because it was raining and they were watching. I thought I would be shot in the back. I didn't look back. I didn't look across my shoulder. When I was 10 metres away from Ismet and Kemal, I heard this man telling them too that they were free to go. And they set off. I heard the men then saying to them, "Run." I heard them starting to walk faster and then there was a burst of gunfire. I looked across my shoulder. I saw Slavenko Balaban firing in the back of my brother and the other man. They fell to the ground, one opposite the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And they were dead?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: They were shot dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether it is appropriate time to have a break because I lost track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much longer do you require? Because from what I read and the documentation that you gave us, you haven't got much left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One hour. Okay. So we'll have a break now of 25 minutes. I take it that if you require one hour, let's make the break for 20 minutes so that you will have an entire one hour afterwards. And I take it that you will conduct the cross-examination tomorrow, then? Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So it's a 20 minutes break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, before the adjournment, we finished with the part where your brother Kemal Alic and Ismet Selimagic were killed. And before you also said that the soldiers separated men from women. At this point, after the death of these two men, where were the rest of you were taken?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, when these people were killed, I approached my family and I stood at the same place, under this balcony. A couple of minutes later from my hamlet of Sikare, they drove out more people, women and children, who had come along the road, whereas we had come across the fields. They ordered people to lie down on the asphalt road. There were about 50 of them. After they lay down, I heard the soldiers saying, "Start with the tank and run them over." But it was only intimidation. Nobody drove the tank at them. Then Dranko -- Branko Balaban, called Sice came, he called out three men, Samid Imsirevic, Camil Alic, and Fehim Mehmedagic. He told them to stand up and they put their hands behind their back and they -- he took them to the road and shot them dead. Then a military vehicle came by. He stopped by. They stopped by and asked us why we were standing there. We said, "The troops ordered to us stand there." They told us that we were free to go towards Japra. We started off --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm really sorry to interrupt you. First thing I forgot to convey you a message from the booths that they would ask to you slow down because they have really a hard time to keep with your speed of talking. So please, slow down. And I will -- I will -- before we will go on with your story, I want to stop when these three men were killed. Did you see it personally?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you -- did they stay on the ground or were they taken somewhere else after they fell down, after they fell down?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: They all remained lying down, those two who were killed earlier, and the three men who were shot later. All of them remained lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So I interrupted you at the point when you said that a military jeep arrived and you were told that you can go wherever you were, or what exactly the person in the car told you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: This person first asked us, "What are you waiting for here?" We replied that the troops had told us to stand there and wait. He cursed the soldiers and said, "You are free to go towards the grounds of the Japra company."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you know this person, the person from the car?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But he was a soldier?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: It was an officer rather than a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And so he sent you towards the Japra compound. So did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We set off along the road towards Japra and we -- when we reached Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the bridge over the Sana River, another group of Serb soldiers was waiting for us there. They were wearing red berets. They told us to empty our pockets on to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I would like to ask the usher to show the witness two photos. It is P1683.44 and 45. You can start with 44 and place it on the ELMO. So can you describe what we can see on this picture?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I can see here the bridge which we were supposed to cross to reach Blagaj Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you show us on the picture which is on the ELMO from which direction you came and in which direction you went?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We came from this direction, took the left turn, crossed the bridge, into Blagaj Rijeka. Here in front of the bridge, we see one side of the road. We don't see the other side on which the soldiers were standing. We threw here on the ground, valuables, papers, gold and jewellery, anything we had, watches. Everything was thrown on to the ground. I didn't throw my car keys. It remained in my pocket. One soldier asked me, "What's in your pocket?" I said the keys of my car. He asked me what kind of car? I told him. And then he made me give him the car keys. After which we were told to go across the bridge into Blagaj Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you show the witness the other picture? So it is the same bridge, just the picture from the different position. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where did you -- on this picture, where did you -- from where did you come?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We came from this direction. And came out on to the bridge. Now we see the other side of the road where the soldiers were standing, as well as on the other side. Here on the road, there were our valuables, papers, and other stuff lying.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with these pictures, and I would like to show the witness pictures 9 -- from 9 until 12. You crossed the bridge and as you stated before, you were ordered to go to Japra compound. What was this Japra compound? What was it?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: It was an enterprise that had a quarry, produced all sorts of construction material, sand, et cetera. You see what kind of material on this picture. This was a mechanical workshop. There was a fence around it. We got off the bridge here and came into the compound, using this entrance, and walked on towards this gate here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At any point, were you taken inside of this building?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had four small children with me and my wife and I came into this building to find cover from the rain. A Serb soldier came in, shot a round through the roof, and told us that all of us men should come out of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you go out?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of us got out and only the women and children remained inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we show the witness other pictures?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We can see the same compound. The other picture, please? Is this -- which side of the warehouse are we seeing now?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: The road was on this side. Here is where we got in. This side is closer to the Sava River and the railway.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While you were outside, did anything occur which struck your attention?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: That same soldier who chased us out came out himself. He was carrying a Kalashnikov this way, with the rifle butt on his shoulder, and he walked about watching us. You don't see the entrance on this picture. But that was where Sulejman Burzic was standing, near the entrance. The soldier asked Sulejman something, I didn't hear exactly what. He asked, "Do you know this man?" Sulejman said yes. And the soldier hit him on his head, and then stepped away from him and fired two rounds into him. Sulejman was shot dead. And then the soldier took a blanket or a plate from somewhere and covered Sulejman's head. He walked by us without saying a word. The soldier's name was Zare Janjetovic. He was the secretary of the local commune in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you repeat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand something here. According to the transcript, we have, "But that was where Sulejman Burzic was standing near the entrance of the soldier asked Sulejman something. I didn't hear exactly what. He asked, Do you know this man? Sulejman said yes and the soldier hit him on his head and then stepped away from him and fired two rounds into him. Sulejman was shot dead." When he asked Sulejman, do you know this man, which man was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The soldier asked, "Do you know who I am?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who you are?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Himself, in other words, he asked Sulejman --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The soldier asked Sulejman, "Do you know who I am?" Sulejman said yes, after which he was hit on the head twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Are you we able to see the place where he was shot on any of these pictures? Maybe the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We can see more clearly here. This is where the fence was, and next to the fence was the road. There was a ramp here. Here was the entrance. It was right at the corner, a metre or two behind the fence that he was standing. I was standing here where this excavator is now, at the time. The distance between us was about 5 metres, not more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm done with these pictures, and if we can prepare pictures 7 and 8. How long did you stay in this compound?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: While we were standing there in the compound, we saw rail cars for livestock that came in a convoy into the Japra compound. We didn't know for which purpose, and later we learned they had been prepared for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So at any point, were you ordered to enter these trains?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: They ordered us to board the rail cars, men to board the open rail cars and women and children the closed ones. Since Ismet was dead, I went to a rail car carrying this disabled aunt of mine. I met Mico at one point and asked him, "Can I board the same rail car as my wife and children and this disabled woman?" He nodded and I boarded a closed rail car together with my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we show these two pictures to the witness? On these two pictures, we can see trains. Are they the same as you boarded?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if they are precisely those, but they are the same kind. We see here the closed rail cars and further down, we see the open type of rail car. When I say "closed," I mean with a roof.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I'm done with these pictures. And you mentioned that you asked one Mico whether you can join your wife. Whom are you referring to? Who was this Mico?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Mico Dolic, who was wearing a military uniform. The same Mico who issued us that ultimatum that day with Ranko Gvozden before we formed a convoy. That's the same Mico who allowed me to come into the same rail car as my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While you were entering, boarding these trains, was -- were you able to observe what went on outside, around these trains?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: When I helped this disabled aunt of mine on to the train, I lay her on the floor, then I looked around to see where my other relatives were, if I could help them board the train, and I'll say the next -- the adjacent rail car was an open type car. I couldn't see. And a soldier came then calling out Hasan Merzihic, who was in one of the adjacent rail cars and came out. The soldier took him towards the creek, towards a small shop there, and when they reached a small bridge at that point, the soldier killed him. Shot him dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see when this Hasan Merzihic was taken away? Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you see when he was shot?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was anybody else taken from this train?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: They called out several people, some failed to respond, and they didn't come in to look for them. I wasn't called out at all. And later we closed the door to prevent our children from watching the scene. I was afraid that somebody might call me out and take me away. I didn't look on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you said some failed to respond. Did anybody respond?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So after you were aboard on these trains, can you describe how many of you were in one wagon, in one of these trains?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly how many we were. We might have been up to a hundred. There were men, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it full or half full?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: The rail car was full. There was this disabled woman. There were sleeping children, people carried luggage. There was not much free space around. It was mainly full.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And where were you taken in this train?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Towards Prijedor, Banja Luka, and Doboj. Right outside Doboj, at a small station, which I had never heard about before, called Stanari, we stopped, and it was only the next --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction it was about 9.00 a.m. in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: We stopped there, we were hungry and thirsty. We asked for water. We needed to change the clothes on our children. We stayed four or five hours there. There were Serb troops around the rail cars and all of a sudden, there came the order for men to be separated from women. We were separated. And then they started loading us into closed rail cars, 140 persons per rail car. At least there were 140 in my rail car. They closed the door behind us. Then we travelled on --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will stop you here for a second. I want to ask you, when you left Bosanski Novi, or this Japra compound, approximately how many rail cars was in your train?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Are you able to tell whether there were five, ten, 20, one?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: There were at least 10 to 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that you -- you travelled until 9.00 in the morning of the following day, that you were thirsty, hungry, you wanted to change your clothes. Were you provided with water, with food?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. We got nothing at all. We went to a creek and we drank there, whether it was fit to drink or not. And then our women changed their babies and washed them there, and they washed their nappies up until to the point where they came and separated us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So after you were separated, you said that you men were loaded to another rail cars. Do you know what happened to the women?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't know. We boarded the closed carriages and we had no notion of what was happening to the women. The women stayed outside and we boarded the carriages, the very same one that the women and children were on earlier on. So we were taken back and we did not know anything about the women and the children, and at a bend, we saw that the open carriages were no longer there. So it was clear to us that the women and children were left behind, that they were not with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you were in these rail cars, in this train, and where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: In the direction of Banja Luka, back to Bosanski Novi. And we got to Banja Luka in late afternoon, early evening, and we were stopped there and Serb soldiers were throwing stones and they were shouting, "This is Alija's army. Open the door so we can cut off their ears." And they swore us in other ways as well. And we kept quiet and we spent the night there in the carriages. And on the day after, in the morning, perhaps around 8.00 or 9.00, of course, I couldn't tell you exactly because we didn't have our watches, we had to relinquish everything. And then we were taken in the direction of Prijedor, Omarska, and we got to Omarska and we just stood there for a long time, and then later on we heard that the plan was to leave us there at Omarska, but then there was apparently no agreement. And then we were taken on to Prijedor and we stayed there as well for about an hour or two, and then we were taken on to Brezicani which is the first station after Prijedor. And then one man opened the doors and he had a hose, and we all went to the water because we wanted a drink of water and it was very hot, and we stayed there for about two hours maybe, and we were told afterwards when we reached the camp that it wouldn't be safe to go through Svodna village because there were some land mines and there were some civilians there who were likely to shoot at the train, and then when some sort of order was re-established --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you but I'm reading, "we were told afterwards, when we reached the camp that it wouldn't be safe to go through Svodna village," et cetera. So I want you to tell us, you were in the train, you were taken in Omarska, you were not received in Omarska, they -- where did they take you from the Omarska? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Prijedor, Brezicani, and then Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So how long this journey lasted? For how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Almost the whole day. We got at the Mlakve stadium at about 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: First you stopped in Doboj when you were close to Doboj, when you were separated from your women? No?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, no. Not in Doboj. Before Doboj, there is a village called Stanari, it is a small railway station, and it's called Stanari.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So it was in the morning and did you reach --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you reach Mlakve stadium the same day?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: On the same day, we got to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So when the train arrived to -- back to Bosanski Novi, where exactly is Mlakve stadium in relation to Bosanski Novi town?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: When you enter Bosanski Novi, there is a railway line to the left and Bihac, Bosanska Krupa, and Odzak are the places which follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how far is the station from the stadium? I'm talking about this railway station where your train stopped.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean? The Bosanski Novi station or Blagaj Japra station?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, what I mean, you said you were taken to Mlakve stadium. So from which station -- from which railway station were you taken to the Mlakve stadium and how far was this railway station from this stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, from the direction of Blagaj, we did not enter the Bosanski Novi station. There was a turnoff. I mean, you could go straight ahead to the railway station but then we went across the bridge, in fact, in the direction of Bihac, and so that railway line is near the stadium and it is about 2 to 3 kilometres, perhaps 2 kilometres. That's the distance between the Bosanski Novi railway station and the Mlakve stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when you were taken to Mlakve stadium from this railway station, were you accompanied by soldiers or did you go on your own?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. We got off there. It was not a railway station. It was just the railway line. And there were canals on both sides. And the doors were opened and then there was an asphalt road to Bihac, and we were asked to cross the road and enter the stadium. And we had the rows of Serb soldiers flanking us as we got off the train and went into the stadium, so basically it was as if you were escorting sheep somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness photos 1 to 6, from 1 until 6. And these are just pictures of Mlakve football stadium. Can you briefly always describe what we can see on these pictures? So you have picture number 1.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: This is the main stadium where we were held. And this is the railing, and this is where the railway line is in the direction of Bihac, as well as the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said you were -- you were held on this field. Do you remember approximately how many -- how many men were kept in that stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I don't remember but it wasn't always easy to tell the precise figure because people were taken away and brought in during the nights, but somewhere around 750, 730. But I can't give you the precise figure, as people were taken away and brought in, and that happened during the night. And then in the morning, you saw new faces people I had not seen before, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you have a look at the second picture? Again, can you tell the Court what we can see and what do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: This is the perimeter and the bleachers and we had guards everywhere, and in the middle, there was another guard, heavily armed, and they were guarding us, watching us, all the time, and around the stadium, there were guards as well, but these, the ones who were here were watching us from an elevated position, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You just said that there were guards. Are you able to tell us whether they were soldiers, regular soldiers, military soldiers, whether they were policemen?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. They were Serb reservists, not regular soldiers, and not the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And on this picture, are we -- are you able to tell us where you were kept?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: The entrance was here behind this woman on the picture here so we went in this way and we slept underneath the bleachers. I can't tell you exactly. And then -- that was the exit. The entrance and the exit. And that's where we could sleep on concrete basically in toilets in the corridors.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will only briefly ask you, you mentioned this entrance. When you enter the Mlakve stadium that day you arrived, were you registered?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody was registered. Names and surnames. And there was a roll call twice a day in the mornings and in the evenings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: While you were in Mlakve stadium, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. I myself wasn't. Some people were. I don't know what about. But I myself was not interrogated, as to the way we were treated, well, they kept cursing us and swearing at us and saying, "Well what was wrong with living with us before?" Et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will go back to conditions in this camp in a moment. I only want to finish the pictures. Can you have a look at the third picture? And can you tell the Court what we can see here.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: You can see the same thing but from the other side. This is the road, and to the left, there is another auxiliary stadium, as it were, and this is where we were, where those glass panels are.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And we can see on this picture some clothes hanging. What were these building which were attached to the main tribune -- to the main building?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: This is the stadium building. There were some apartments there and some of them were even inhabited whilst we were being held there, but for the most part they were inhabited by Serbs. There were no Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that some Serbs lived there. Were you able to contact them?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. By no means.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Picture number 4. What is this? Is it the main field or is it that auxiliary field?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. This is the auxiliary one. This is the auxiliary one. Behind this here you can see -- behind is the river Una and behind there, across the river, it's the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that there is the territory of Croatia. Were you able to establish any contact from the outside world?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. We were there but on the previous picture, where you can see a glass panels, I mean people were looking across at Una and the UN noticed it and they would come by, they would come by cars, and since there is a road behind the river, and there were people passing by and then they would turn their cars. And people would come to the windows to the glass panels, and those driving by in their cars were flashing their lights and greeting us and when the Serbs realised, they made it impossible afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that there were UN. Do you know what kind of people they were?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. It's just that when we were released from the stadium, when we went in the direction of Croatia, I saw blue helmets. I didn't know who or what they were, but they escorted us all the way to Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Then we have picture number 5. It is again the main field, which -- and we can see the houses. Were these houses -- did these houses belong to Muslims or to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: It was a mixed population. There were both Serbs and Muslims there. It was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm done with the pictures. Now I would like to ask you about the conditions in this camp. You already said that you had to sleep on the floor. Did you have any blankets?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No blankets to speak of, no, no blankets. You simply had to lie down where there was enough space. If there was not enough space to lie down, you had to sit up. There were 730 or 750 people. There was not enough space for all of us and people got head lice. We couldn't wash properly. We had to wash with cold water, without soap, and sometimes there was not even water, there was no electricity. I mean, the conditions were hopeless.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What about meals? Did you receive your meal regularly and how often?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No. We had a meal in the morning and another one in the evening, but one kilo of bread would be divided amongst eight people. If it's fresh bread, it's just one slice, and it's two pieces basically each, and then the soup was so thin and it just looked like dish water, like when you do the dishes, and the water that remains. That's what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And apart from the soup, did you receive -- soup and bread, did you receive something else?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. And sometimes we were given salt in boxes, and sometimes I put some salt in a piece of paper. And since I didn't have anything to eat, I would just eat a bit of salt because otherwise I couldn't even drink and I didn't have any bread and for 28 days, I didn't even use the toilet because we didn't have enough to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How were you treated by the guards in this camp?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended. We had different people there every week. Some of them were all right. Sometimes they were taunting us. They would bring along cigarettes and said that they could -- we could buy them, but we didn't have any money, or then they said they would search us and if they found any money, they would kill us. And then they opened the packets and would sell cigarettes one by one just so that they could get everything that we had out of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During your stay in the camp, were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I myself wasn't beaten but some people were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was anybody injured while in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes and no. I mean, I once saw an underage boy being hit, and he was hit in the stomach with a gun, that's something that I witnessed. Perhaps there were other instances that I did not witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was there anybody ill during the stay in the camp? And was any medical help provided, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Some people were ill, but nobody provided any medical assistance. You were sick, you were sick. There was nobody to complain to or ask for anything. You just lasted as long as you could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know whether doctors or a doctor ever come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as I'm aware, no. I only know that there was somebody employed at the hospital once came along, and he gave us a powder to stop the head lice spreading, but he didn't do it. They just gave us this spray, the powder. And then the following day, they brought a tank of cold water so that we could wash out the powder. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you sustain any injury while in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: I had a problem in my right eye. A Serb soldier hit me. I don't know who he was. I don't know his name. But I still can't see from that eye. It was already dark, almost night-time, and I didn't see who hit me, and the eye remained closed until I got to Croatia. When I came to Croatia, I went to the doctor. They tried to treat me and then I had surgery when I was in Germany, but I -- I've lost my sight in that eye.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: On the 9th, we came out, so 45 days, a month and a half. We left the houses on the 9th of June, and on the 11th of June, we entered the camp, and on the 23rd of August, we left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before you left the camp, did you sign any papers?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had to sign a paper stating that we were leaving the municipality of Bosanski Novi permanently, voluntarily, and that we left all our belongings to the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This piece of paper you just described, did you sign it in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. camp?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Everybody had to sign.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And who brought this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: It came from the municipality, from the Crisis Staff. The people who came along were civilians so I don't know who they were. They had two desks and we were -- we were just filing by and putting our signatures on to these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that they came, they had two desks. Were they civilians or soldiers or were they in civilian clothes or in uniforms, these people who brought --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: They were civilians. They had civilian clothing and they had some folders, some papers, and they put all that on to the desks. Everything had been prepared in advance. All we had to do was put our signatures.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to show the witness one other document. It's the new one, P1627. And it says, among others, "Client Midho Alic, Declaration, I hereby declare that I own no real estate in Bosanski Novi municipality, under my own name, and that I am permanently leaving Bosanski Novi municipality." We can see that the signature is not yours. Who was the person who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: In the course of my stay at the stadium, I lived in Blagaj and I had somebody here and she knew that it was possible to get those papers and that people would be released on the basis of them, and she came along one day, she brought some bread. Sometimes people were allowed to bring food, sometimes they were not. So I managed to be in touch with her, and I told her to sign the papers for me and her name was Mujic, Minka. She is a cousin of mine -- or rather my sister. Because I didn't have anything to my name. It was all in my father's name. All the property I did have, my house and my father had his house, but it was all in his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And at the end, you were released on 27 of -- I'm sorry, 23rd of July, and you were put on convoy, is it correct, and you were taken to Karlovac and then further?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We crossed the Una river and we crossed over into Croatia, the place called Dvor, and then across Glina, we got to Karlovac. We were taken by bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have three documents which I can finish in five minutes but most probably tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we have to stop here, otherwise, we will create problems for the Trial Chamber that will start at quarter past 2.00. Mr. Alic, I thank you for your patience and your cooperation. We haven't finished. Madam Richterova has got only a few minutes left, and then you will be taken over on cross-examination by Mr. Trbojevic, I suppose, and that will be tomorrow morning, starting at 9.00, for which time this sitting is being adjourned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
